title: I'm rebuilding my 10-year-old game from scratch.
author: TallonZek
selftext:
Heya people,

I released [Rubber and Lead](https://store.steampowered.com/app/389810/Rubber_and_Lead/) back in 2015. My gamedev path: I got fired, messed around with Unity and Playmaker for a few days, and had an "aha" moment (I'd done some modding before) where I thought "I can do this, let's make a game." So I did. I taught myself, and it took nearly a year to release.

This was back in the Greenlight days. My Greenlight submission attracted an artist and we worked together on a rev share. The game made some money and got finished, so it's a success on those terms, but it had real shortcomings. It's sitting at 43 reviews with a Mixed score, and it deserves it.

Most of the problems came from my lack of skill at expressing my ideas back then, and from severe crunch at the end. I was living off savings and loans from family and pushed very hard to finish. After release I found out the hard way that I crash badly after finishing a project. I turned my back on it for about six months, and when I came back, the pile of technical debt from Playmaker was too much to dig into.

I did finish a game without writing code though. Playmaker let me build everything as state machines (FSMs), more like flowcharts than a codebase. I've always been bad at both art and code but decent at design. Looking back, Playmaker was a much cruder version of the kind of help AI gives now.

I recently wrapped up a non-video-game project and was deciding what to do next. I have a prototype I want to turn into a full game, but I thought, what the hell, let's have Claude look at my old project first.

I dug a copy of the files out of an old laptop (thankful I still had them): the shipped build plus an older project backup. Claude decompiled the build and decoded all \~7,500 Playmaker state machines back into readable logic. That recovered the whole design, including every car's stats, weapon damage, arena prizes, XP curves and all 60-odd courier jobs. For me it's on the level of the Rosetta Stone.

So now I'm going full No Man's Sky. I'm rebuilding it from scratch in Godot: 3D instead of 2D, more systems, and the original design finally done properly. Then I'll archive the current build as a legacy branch and release the new version on the same store page. I care less about money than about building it to match the original vision.

The workflow so far: Claude for design recovery and planning, agents in Godot plus Blender over MCP for building, and everything kept in the repo so I can swap models when usage runs out. Happy to share more on any of it.

comments.author: denhopeEUW
comments.body: This is great - good example what is possible with AI. Keep it up

replies.author: TallonZek
replies.body: Yea the new models are genuinely impressive. It's the first time I've interacted with them and thought 'this mf is smarter than me'.

replies.author: orellanaed
replies.body: If you're using Godot already look into Flockbay. Useful harness for using Claude Code via MCP. More token efficient

replies.author: TallonZek
replies.body:
Thanks for the tip I'll check it out, I've been flipping between claude code and codex/astra as usage dictates.

Claude reports that we're currently using coding-solo's godot mcp and recommended sticking with it.

comments.author: Big_Presentation2786
comments.body: What were your original sales like?

replies.author: TallonZek
replies.body: total revenue over about 3 years I want to say was around $10,000, it made money but not enough to justify a year of work. It also could have done better if I had supported it with patches etc. but I just wasn't up to it at the time. Original price was 4.99 I dropped it to a dollar a couple years back.

replies.author: Big_Presentation2786
replies.body:
That's actually a HUGE potential..

Good stuff.

Hope the rebuild goes great for you..

replies.author: TallonZek
replies.body: Thanks! I'm stoked about redeeming the game and fully enjoying the new project honeymoon phase hehe.

replies.author: Big_Presentation2786
replies.body: Instead of rebuilding it, make a sequel (or prequel) you'll then be able to guage your skill and improvement..

replies.author: TallonZek
replies.body:
I thought about that but don't think it's really good enough to 'deserve' a sequel. I think replacing the product with a superior version is a better goodwill gesture, and it also brings some very relevant discussion (I think) to the space.

My thought process is that if I release an AI assisted version, that is clearly superior to the version I originally released, and is free for current owners, that should if not deflect AI hate at least provide some interesting responses to it, such as the original also being made without coding or art skills.

I'll need to clear things with Valve first, and likely will need to redo my AI-disclosure, as that didn't exist at the time I originally released.

replies.author: denhopeEUW
replies.body: This is the way. When you get good feedback and attention you can still develop a new game or a sequel.
